statement: If X_n converges to X in distribution, then X_n converges to X in probability.
definitions: X_n and X are real random variables on a common probability space; X_n -> X in distribution means F_{X_n}(t) -> F_X(t) at all continuity points t of F_X; X_n -> X in probability means P(|X_n - X| > eps) -> 0 for every eps > 0.
ground_truth_witness: Let X be uniform on {0,1} and X_n = 1 - X for every n. Each X_n has exactly the law of X, so X_n -> X in distribution trivially; but |X_n - X| = |1 - 2X| = 1 with probability one, so P(|X_n - X| >= 1/2) = 1 for every n and X_n does not converge to X in probability.
reference_authority: published counterexample (book-cited), verified per partB_feasibility records
book_citation: J. M. Stoyanov, Counterexamples in Probability, Wiley, 1987 (3rd ed., Dover, 2013); chapter on limit theorems, section on various kinds of convergence (convergence in distribution does not yield convergence in probability); example number not pinned from freely available sources.
